mappings.note: Recall of the Sinhala share of Sri Lanka's population. Not LO-3, which asks for analysis of the majoritarian MEASURES; this asks only for the demographic fact that makes a Sinhala majority possible. The frame offers no recall-level LO for case-study demography, so the recall competency C-3.1 is the honest level.
Asks what majoritarianism LED TO, i.e. the consequence, so LO-4 (consequences and growth of alienation into conflict) rather than LO-3, which is about identifying the measures themselves.

Concurrent List: both Union and State may legislate. That is the vertical form of power sharing between levels of government, which is LO-2's subject. Not LO-1, which asks WHY sharing is desirable rather than what forms exist.

Pure institutional recall (the Mayor heads a Municipal Corporation). Not LO-2: the item does not ask the candidate to analyse local government as a form of power sharing, only to name its head. No recall-level LO exists in this 6-LO frame.
Identifying which country is federal is identifying a form of power sharing found in modern democracies, LO-2. Not C-3.2, which is about applying understanding to contemporary situations.
Holding-together versus coming-together federation is a distinction between forms of power sharing, LO-2. Not LO-1 (desirability) and not C-3.3 (evaluating outcomes).

Recall of where Sri Lanka's Indian Tamils are concentrated. Not LO-3 or LO-4: no measure and no consequence is in question, only the location of a community. Competency-level citation because the frame has no recall LO.

Names the city (Brussels) where Dutch-French tension was sharpest. Descriptive recall of the Belgian case, not LO-2 (which is about the arrangements adopted) and not LO-6 (which evaluates the outcome).

Asks the cause of Dutch-French tension (the wealthier, better-educated French-speaking minority). The frame's Belgian LO, LO-6, evaluates the OUTCOME; nothing in the frame covers the pre-existing cleavage, so the recall/understanding competency is cited.
Percentage of Belgians in the Flemish region: demographic recall. Not LO-2, which concerns the power-sharing arrangements rather than the population split.
Names the Dutch-speaking community as the one resenting French-speaking dominance. Recall of the Belgian cleavage, not an evaluation of the Belgian outcome (LO-6).
Duplicate stem of qid:105360, same reasoning: demographic recall of the Sinhala share, below the analytic level of LO-3.
Defining majoritarianism is exactly LO-3's second half, how a democratic majority can act unjustly. Chosen over bare C-3.1 because the concept named IS the LO's concept, not mere case detail.
Consequence of the majoritarian policy, so LO-4 not LO-3. Duplicate stem of qid:105361.

The original Sri Lankan Tamil demands (recognition of Tamil, regional autonomy, equality in jobs and education) are the alienation LO-4 traces. Not LO-3, which is about the Sinhala majority's measures rather than the Tamil response.

How Belgium solved its ethnic problem = the community government, equal ministers and Brussels arrangement, i.e. the forms of power sharing LO-2 asks about. LO-6 would fit an item that JUDGED that solution; this one asks what it was.
Elements of vertical power sharing are a direct test of the forms of power sharing, LO-2. Not LO-1 (desirability).
Elements of horizontal power sharing: same LO-2 as the vertical item, since the LO covers the taxonomy of forms as a whole.
Identifying what is NOT an element of majoritarianism tests the concept LO-3 builds on. Not LO-4: no consequence is in question.

Asks which reason for power sharing is invalid, so the target is the case FOR power sharing, LO-1. Not LO-5, which asks specifically for the prudential/moral distinction; this item does not sort reasons into those two kinds.
Belgium's bordering countries: geographical recall from the case study. No LO in this frame reaches below the analytic level, so the recall competency is cited.
80 per cent of Brussels speaks French: demographic recall. Not LO-2, which concerns the arrangement Brussels received rather than its language split.
The complementary 20 per cent Dutch-speaking figure for Brussels. Same recall level as qid:105391.

Asks what made Brussels a special problem (a French-speaking majority in a Dutch-majority country). Understanding of the case's difficulty, not yet an analysis of the arrangement (LO-2) or of the outcome (LO-6).
Tamil-speaking share of Sri Lanka's population: demographic recall, below LO-3's analytic level.
Recall of the term 'Indian Tamils' for the descendants of colonial-era plantation workers. Terminology recall, not the majoritarian measures of LO-3.
Most Sinhala speakers are Buddhist: recall of the religious composition. It matters for the Buddhism-fostering measure, but this item asks only the fact, not the measure (LO-3).
Date of Sri Lankan independence (1948). Chronological recall; LO-3 concerns what the majority did AFTER independence.
The 1956 Sinhala-only Act plus preferential university and government-job policies are the majoritarian measures LO-3 names explicitly. Not LO-4, which covers what those measures produced.
The word to be filled is 'alienation', LO-4's exact subject: how the measures grew into estrangement. Not LO-3, which is the measures themselves.
The 1980s demand for a separate Tamil Eelam is the point where alienation became secessionist, squarely LO-4's trajectory.
End of the civil war (2009): the terminus of the conflict LO-4 traces. Not LO-6, which weighs the outcome against the legitimacy claim rather than dating it.
How many times Belgium amended its constitution between 1970 and 1993: recall about the construction of the Belgian power-sharing model, so LO-2 rather than LO-6's evaluation of its result.
Equal numbers of Dutch- and French-speaking ministers in the central government is a named feature of the Belgian model, i.e. a form of power sharing, LO-2.
The community government's powers over culture, education and language are a third, community-level form of power sharing, LO-2's subject. Not LO-6, which judges the Belgian result.
Asks for a reason power sharing is good for a country, which is LO-1 verbatim. Not LO-5, which requires the prudential/moral distinction to be drawn; the item accepts either kind.
Asks specifically for a MORAL reason, so this is LO-5's prudential/moral distinction and not the undifferentiated desirability of LO-1.
Power sharing emerged in opposition to the notion of undivided political power: the rationale for sharing, LO-1. Not LO-2, since no particular form is named.
Asks for an example of horizontal distribution of power, a form of power sharing, LO-2.
Names the system of checks and balances among legislature, executive and judiciary. A form of power sharing, LO-2, not a reason for it (LO-1).
Four-statement item comparing Belgium's federal transformation with Sri Lanka's majoritarianism. LO-6 is the only LO that puts the two outcomes side by side; LO-3 and LO-4 cover Sri Lanka alone.
Christian share of Sri Lanka's population (7 per cent, both Tamil and Sinhala): demographic recall, below the analytic LOs.
The missing word is 'majoritarian', describing the measures adopted to establish Sinhala supremacy: LO-3, not LO-4's consequences.
The constitutional duty to protect and foster Buddhism is one of the enumerated majoritarian measures, LO-3. (Stem is garbled: the trailing words 'Tamil Indians' belong to a different item.)
Brussels as the EU headquarters: incidental recall from the Belgian case study. No LO covers it; the recall competency is the honest level.
Sorts seven statements into arguments for and against power sharing, i.e. the case for its desirability, LO-1. Not LO-5: the item does not ask which reasons are prudential and which moral.

Two-statement item on power sharing being good for democracy and reducing inter-group conflict: the desirability claim of LO-1. LO-5 would require the candidate to label the conflict-reduction reason as prudential, which this item does not ask.
